0.title: Using Our Tools Without Being Used by Them
0.essay:
Most of us now carry a device that connects us to the whole world. It brings news, friends, music, maps, sermons and the entire Bible in one pocket. It also brings constant interruption, endless entertainment, pornography, comparison, outrage, and the temptation never to be silent or alone with our thoughts.

Shaped by our phones

Many Christians sense that their phones are shaping them more than they would like, but they are not sure what to do about it.

What Scripture offers

The Bible does not mention smartphones, social media or artificial intelligence. But it says a great deal about the heart, the mind, attention, speech, community, rest and idolatry. Those principles apply to every new technology.

Not evil, not neutral

Technology is not evil. Human beings were made to develop God’s world, and tools are part of that calling. But tools are never neutral. They shape the people who use them. The question for Christians is not whether to use technology, but how to use it wisely, so that it serves God’s purposes rather than our idols.

The chapters

Tools and the Heart; Attention and the Mind; Social Media and the Self; Mastered by Nothing; and Embodied People in a Digital Age.

For reflection

What is the first thing you reach for in the morning, and the last thing at night? What might that say about your heart?

1.title: Tools and the Heart
1.essay:
Tools are a gift from God. But every tool can serve pride, and every tool shapes the person who uses it.

Tools are a gift

God made human beings to “fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). Developing tools, crafts and technology is part of that calling. In Genesis 4, Cain’s descendants developed livestock farming, music and metalworking (Genesis 4:20–22). Noah built an ark. The tabernacle was built by skilled craftsmen, and God said of Bezalel, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Technology is a good part of human culture.

Yet the same chapter of Genesis that records the first musicians and metalworkers also records growing violence (Genesis 4:23–24). Technology advances, but the heart still needs redemption.

Tools can serve pride

At Babel, people used a new technology, baked bricks, to build a city and a tower. They said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). The problem was not the bricks but the heart. Technology can be used to glorify ourselves, and to try to reach heaven without God. At Babel, it ended in confusion.

Tools shape us

Psalm 115 says of idols, “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). We become like what we worship. In a similar way, we are shaped by what we give our time and attention to. Constant scrolling trains us to be distracted. Instant answers train us to be impatient. Endless entertainment trains us to be bored by anything slow.

Guard your heart

“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The father in Proverbs goes on: “Let your eyes look directly forward” (Proverbs 4:25). Technology enters the heart through the eyes and ears. What we watch, read and listen to shapes what we love and desire. Wisdom is largely a matter of what we let in.

Idols in our pockets

An idol is anything we look to for what only God can give: identity, security, comfort, meaning. Phones and screens can become idols when they are where we turn first for comfort or meaning, when we reach for them in boredom, loneliness or anxiety instead of reaching for God.

Neither fear nor worship

Some Christians fear all new technology. Others embrace it uncritically. Both are mistaken. Technology is a tool under God, to be used with wisdom and gratitude. Unbelievers create many good technologies, and God gives wisdom to farmers and craftsmen of every kind: “his God teaches him” (Isaiah 28:26). Christians can thank God for medical advances, communication and knowledge, whoever developed them.

When the printing press was invented in the fifteenth century, Bibles and pamphlets could be printed cheaply for the first time. The Reformation spread rapidly through printed materials, and ordinary people could read Scripture in their own language. God used a new technology for the gospel.

The right questions

Christians can ask of any technology: Does it help me love God and my neighbour? Does it make me more like Christ? Does it serve my calling, or distract me from it? Does it master me? And what does it cost me, in time, attention, relationships or purity?

Think of a Christian who notices that the first thing he does each morning is check his phone, and the last thing each night is scroll. He decides to charge his phone outside the bedroom, and to begin each day with Scripture and prayer before looking at a screen. His mornings change, and so does his spirit.

For reflection

How has technology shaped your habits and desires, for good and ill? What questions could you ask about a new app or device before you start using it?

2.title: Attention and the Mind
2.essay:
Attention is one of our most precious resources. What we pay attention to shapes what we love, who we become and how we spend our lives. And many modern technologies are designed to capture and hold it for as long as possible.

Love and attention

We give attention to what we love, and we come to love what we give attention to. In that sense, attention is a form of worship. So it matters enormously where it goes.

Set your minds

“Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth” (Colossians 3:2). Believers have been raised with Christ, and their life is hidden with him. Their attention belongs where their true life is. Christians are called to direct their attention deliberately towards Christ.

Think about these things

“Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). That is a filter for what we watch, read and dwell on. Paul goes on to promise that the God of peace will be with those who practise it (Philippians 4:9). Our thoughts shape our peace.

Turn my eyes

The psalmist prayed, “Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways” (Psalm 119:37), and “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!” (Psalm 119:36). Much of what fills our screens is worthless: trivia, gossip, outrage and noise. Some of it is worse. And attention is something we must ask God to direct; we cannot manage it by willpower alone.

Be still

“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Stillness is increasingly rare. Many people never sit in silence, never have an unoccupied moment, never let their minds wander into prayer. Yet stillness is where we often hear God most clearly through his word.

Constant distraction can also be a way of avoiding God, ourselves and our sin. Silence makes us face what is really in our hearts. That is uncomfortable, but it is necessary for growth.

Even at the height of his ministry, with crowds pressing in, Jesus “would withdraw to desolate places and pray” (Luke 5:16). He made space for silence with his Father.

Martha and Mary

When Jesus visited their home, “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40), while Mary sat at his feet and listened. Jesus said, “Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Martha’s problem was not hard work but distraction. Sitting still with Christ is the one necessary thing.

Deep reading

The blessed person delights in God’s law, “and on his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). Meditation requires slow, focused attention. Constant skimming and switching can weaken our capacity to read deeply, including our capacity to read the Bible well.

Stewarding time

“Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:15–16). Our time is a gift from God, and we will give account of how we used it.

Practical steps

Turn off unnecessary notifications. Keep phones away during meals, conversations and worship. Set times of the day free from screens. Read Scripture from a printed Bible if your phone distracts you. Practise silence and prayer, even for a few minutes at first.

Think of a young mother who finds she reaches for her phone whenever the children are quiet. She feels scattered and anxious. She decides to leave the phone in a drawer during the children’s nap, and to use that time for prayer, reading and rest. She is surprised how much calmer she becomes.

For reflection

When did you last sit in silence for ten minutes without a screen? Use Philippians 4:8 as a filter: what would you stop watching or reading?

3.title: Social Media and the Self
3.essay:
Social media can connect us with distant friends, spread good news and share the gospel. It can also feed some of our worst tendencies.

Seeking approval

Paul asked, “For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). Living for the approval of others and living for Christ are incompatible.

Social media constantly tests where we seek approval. It rewards us with likes and followers, quietly training us to live for the applause of others.

Think of a Christian student who realises she checks how many likes her posts get dozens of times a day, and feels low when a post does poorly. She takes a month off social media, and discovers how much of her self-worth had come from it. When she returns, she uses it more sparingly and no longer counts likes.

Performing righteousness

Jesus warned, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). Those who do so have their reward already: human applause. Instead, “when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:6).

Posting our good deeds, spiritual experiences or perfect family moments can easily become a way of seeking praise. The hidden life of faith is safe from vanity.

Comparison

Social media shows us the highlights of other people’s lives. We compare our ordinary days with their best moments, and envy grows. “A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot” (Proverbs 14:30).

A given identity

Social media invites us to build and curate an identity. But a Christian’s identity is given, not built. “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). We are children of God. We do not need to perform to be accepted.

Speech

Online, people say things they would never say face to face. Anonymity and distance make it easy to be harsh, mocking or careless. But “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Paul goes on to list bitterness, wrath, clamour and slander as things to put away. Every word we type is still speech before God.

Outrage

Much online content is designed to provoke anger, because anger keeps us scrolling. James gives a perfect rule for online life: “let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). Christians should not be swept along by the latest outrage.

Truth

Misinformation spreads quickly online. “The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). Christians should share only what is true, checking before passing things on. Spreading falsehood, even unknowingly, breaks the ninth commandment.

Privacy and wisdom

Christians should think carefully about what they share about themselves and others, especially children. Not everything needs to be public.

Good uses

Social media can be used well: to encourage friends, share Scripture, pray for others, support mission and maintain real relationships. The question is whether we use it, or it uses us. Before posting, it helps to ask: Why am I sharing this? Would I say this face to face? Does it build up?

For reflection

Where do you seek approval most: from God, or from others online? How should Ephesians 4:29 shape what you post and comment?

4.title: Mastered by Nothing
4.essay:
Many technologies are not sinful in themselves. But anything that masters us has become a problem.

Lawful but not helpful

The Corinthians had a slogan: “All things are lawful.” Paul agreed in part, but added two qualifications: not everything is helpful, “but I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Christian freedom includes freedom from compulsions.

Christians are free from legalistic rules about technology. But freedom is not licence: “only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (Galatians 5:13).

Signs of being mastered

We are mastered when we cannot stop, when we feel anxious without our device, when it crowds out prayer, Scripture, work or relationships, or when we hide how much we use it. Gaming, streaming, scrolling and online shopping can all become compulsive. A simple test: is there any technology you could not give up for a week? What does that tell you?

Think of a father who realises he spends most evenings gaming after the children are in bed, and that his wife feels neglected. He confesses this to her, limits gaming to one evening a week, and begins spending evenings talking with her and reading. Their marriage grows closer.

Pornography

The internet has made pornography instantly accessible, and many Christians struggle with it. It is not a small issue. Jesus said that lustful looking is adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Pornography damages marriages, distorts views of sex, exploits real people and enslaves those who use it.

But there is forgiveness and freedom in Christ. Practical steps such as filters, accountability and removing access are wise, alongside dealing with the heart. The Fighting Sin and Biblical Sexuality studies address this more fully.

Filled with the Spirit

“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). What fills and controls us matters. The Spirit, not any substance or device, should govern our lives. Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). It is not mere willpower, but the Spirit’s work in us as we depend on him and use wise means.

Small habits

Small daily habits shape character over time. Changing technology habits may seem trivial, but it can have deep effects on the soul. Daniel and his friends lived in the most powerful culture of their day without being mastered by it, and it began with a simple decision about what they would eat (Daniel 1:8–16).

Children and screens

Parents are responsible for what their children see and how technology shapes them. “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Proverbs 22:6). Wise boundaries, supervision, and above all modelling good habits, matter. Parents cannot teach what they do not practise.

Rest

When the apostles returned from their mission, so busy they had no time even to eat, Jesus said, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). He cares about rest. Constant connectivity can rob us of real rest. A weekly break from screens, especially on the Lord’s Day, can restore body and soul.

To the glory of God

“So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Paul gave this principle while discussing Christian freedom and the good of others. It includes how we use our phones and computers. Every use of technology can be measured by it.

For reflection

Which technology do you feel most mastered by? What practical boundaries could help you use it wisely? How could a weekly break from screens benefit you and your household?

5.title: Embodied People in a Digital Age
5.essay:
Human beings are not minds trapped in bodies. God made us embodied creatures, and he saved us by coming in a body. Presence matters.

God made bodies

“The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). We are embodied creatures, and our bodies matter to God.

The Word became flesh

God did not save us by sending a message from a distance. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). God’s ultimate communication was not a message but a person, present in a body. Jesus touched lepers, ate with sinners, washed feet and wept with friends. Presence is at the heart of the gospel.

So love is shown most fully in presence: sitting with the sick, sharing a meal, embracing the grieving. Technology can support presence, but it is a poor substitute for it.

Face to face

John wrote, “Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete” (2 John 12). Letters were good, but presence completed joy. The same is true of digital communication today. Paul, who wrote so many letters, still told the Romans, “For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you” (Romans 1:11).

The gathered church

Hebrews urges believers to “consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:24–25). Online services can be a real help to the housebound. But they cannot replace the gathered body: singing together, sharing the Lord’s Supper, embracing, serving and being known.

Think of a church that moved its services online during a crisis, and found that some members never returned in person. The elders visit each one, explaining why gathering matters. Many come back and rediscover the joy of worshipping together. Those who cannot come are visited regularly.

Artificial intelligence

New tools can now write, answer questions and imitate human conversation. They can be useful for research, work and learning. But they are tools, not persons. They have no soul, no conscience and no relationship with God.

Christians should use them wisely, check what they produce, never treat them as a source of truth equal to Scripture, and never let them replace human relationships, prayer, or the work of thinking for ourselves. True wisdom comes from God: “For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2:6).

Human dignity

As machines become more capable, some will suggest that humans are no more than complex machines. Scripture insists that human beings are made in God’s image, with a dignity no machine can share.

Truth and discernment

In an age of faked images and misinformation, Christians must be people of truth, careful with what they believe and share: “test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

The resurrection

Our hope is not to escape the body into a digital or purely spiritual existence. It is the resurrection of the body and a renewed earth. “For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). The future is embodied: face to face with God, and with one another.

For reflection

Are your closest relationships mostly online or face to face? What could you do this week to be more physically present with family, friends and church?
